added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
added_claims.quote: the ECB I think has caught eight times since 2024 uh about 200 basis points
added_claims.claim: Long-end yields hit multi-decade highs even though the ECB had cut about 200 basis points in eight cuts since 2024, so the long end is pricing something other than policy rates (fiscal supply), in a soft economy that Niels compares to 2022.
added_claims.indicator: UK 30-year gilt, German long yields, US 30-year vs ECB policy rate
added_claims.direction: long-end yields up while policy rates fall (steepening)
added_claims.conditions: A 2022-like bond selloff favors trend following.
added_claims.testable: yes - long yields vs policy rate path

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
added_claims.quote: a market where uh even big managers can take reasonable precise positions
added_claims.claim: Gold is liquid enough for even the largest CTAs to hold meaningful positions, so a gold trend lifts the whole trend-following industry, unlike smaller commodity trends large funds cannot capture.
added_claims.indicator: gold futures liquidity and CTA capacity
added_claims.conditions: Capacity differs by market; small markets cap fund size.
added_claims.testable: partly - capacity can be estimated from volume

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
added_claims.quote: only a few months ago there were uh articles coming out um very disappointed with the returns of of our beloved industry
added_claims.claim: Trend-following performance turns sharply and the narrative lags: after disappointed press in spring 2025 returns recovered within months, so judging the strategy on short windows misleads.
added_claims.conditions: Trend returns are lumpy and arrive with the regime change.

added_claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
added_claims.quote: that is simply because we haven't found a good way to access them
added_claims.claim: Market selection is limited by access and operational complexity: very small emerging carbon markets (e.g. New Zealand) are excluded because setting them up is time-intensive and adds operational risk, not because of weak trend properties.
added_claims.conditions: Added only when a workable execution and clearing route exists.

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
added_claims.quote: if you if you have large AUM you need to do something that gradually moves risk
added_claims.claim: Large managers may prefer smoother indicators (moving averages) because they let risk be scaled in and out gradually; Moritz replies that the same smoothing can be achieved with several look-back windows on simple indicators.
added_claims.indicator: moving average vs derivative-free breakout signals
added_claims.testable: partly - compare signal families at different capacity

added_claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
added_claims.quote: if we could improve this and move from 70 to 60 to 50% losing trades, our returns would go through the roof
added_claims.claim: Lowering the share of losing trades from 70% to 60% or 50% would lift returns sharply, but nothing statistically significant has been found that beats entering on a new high, so entry improvement is the research bottleneck.
added_claims.conditions: Win rate is about 30% in a positively skewed return stream.

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
added_claims.quote: whether it makes a big difference in the very long run um I don't know because sometimes it can be hard to see the difference
added_claims.claim: Differences between position-sizing approaches (no resizing, vol-based, risk-based) are hard to see in very long-run manager performance, though they differ along the way.
added_claims.conditions: Visible in individual years and drawdowns, not in long-run totals.
added_claims.testable: yes - compare sizing variants over the same market set

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
added_claims.quote: that could also be driven by as you say market universe which is clearly very important uh in determining um managers returns
added_claims.claim: The market universe a CTA trades is a major driver of its returns, so differences between managers often come from what they trade rather than sizing details.
added_claims.conditions: Man Group dispersion paper is mentioned as a source.
added_claims.testable: yes - attribute manager returns to market universe

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
added_claims.quote: single day or two-day event risk where you can just get stopped out if you if you use that kind of approach
added_claims.claim: Niels counters the 'punchiness' case: not resizing leaves event risk (a position can be stopped out on a one-or-two-day move), while vol-based sizing trims positions in vol bursts but rebuilds them when vol falls, so the difference is more nuanced than portrayed.
added_claims.indicator: dynamic position sizing vs fixed sizing
added_claims.direction: positions cut in vol bursts and re-added later
added_claims.conditions: Depends on how quickly vol decays after a shock.
added_claims.testable: yes - compare sizing rules around shock events

added_claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
added_claims.quote: you would be able to increase the overall portfolio returns and decrease the overall portfolio risk
added_claims.claim: Lintner's 1987 paper (caption 'John Lindner') argued that adding non-correlated managed futures to stocks and bonds raises portfolio return and lowers risk, the original diversification case that the Don Capital paper extends to 14 alternatives.
added_claims.indicator: managed futures allocation in stock/bond portfolio
added_claims.conditions: Needs low or negative correlation to equities and bonds.

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
added_claims.quote: actually it's probably more the loss you can experience that is the real risk
added_claims.claim: Volatility is a poor risk measure for investors; the real risk is the loss one can experience, so the study compares maximum drawdown relative to volatility, where trend following ranks first.
added_claims.conditions: Trend following has high vol but contained drawdowns relative to it.
added_claims.testable: yes - ratio computed for each strategy

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen (host)
added_claims.quote: So we're not cherry-picking uh as such. We're just saying this is the criteria.
added_claims.claim: Crisis windows were defined by a fixed rule (S&P 500 drawdown of 20-25% or more), which gives only four episodes since 2000, so the result is rule-based but a very small sample.
added_claims.indicator: S&P 500 drawdown above 20-25% as crisis definition

added_claims.speaker: Moritz (guest, CTA/commodity trend follower)
added_claims.quote: one thing that was very different back then was they didn't mind the volatility
added_claims.claim: Early sovereign-wealth allocators that seeded today's largest CTAs tolerated high volatility; today's institutions do not, even though long horizons should make volatility irrelevant, so the shift is behavioural and driven by allocator incentives.
added_claims.conditions: Applies to allocators judged annually on peer-relative performance.
